title: New York State Launches AI Safety Law Targeting OpenAI, Anthropic, Mandating Incident Reports Within 72 Hours
summary: New York State launches AI safety law mandating incident reports within 72 hours
detailed: New York State is launching the RAISE Act, requiring frontier AI developers with over $500 million in annual revenue to register by January 1 and report major safety incidents within 72 hours.

Enforcement is managed by the Division of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust (DIGIT), with first violations carrying penalties up to $1 million and subsequent violations up to $3 million.
The state also established the New York AI Responsibility and Research Center at Binghamton University with $55 million in backing to independently assess AI safety systems.

This matters for tech product managers because differing state reporting deadlines, such as New York's 72 hours versus California's 15 days, require multi-state operators to build robust, strict compliance systems.
sentences: New York State is moving to fully activate safety regulations aimed at large artificial intelligence (AI) developers.
Frontier AI companies with annual revenues exceeding $500 million (~670 billion won) must register with state authorities by January 1 of next year and report major safety incidents within 72 hours.
On the 10th (local time), New York State opened a corporate registration portal ahead of the implementation of the RAISE Act, an AI safety and transparency bill.
The RAISE Act takes effect early next year.
Frontier AI refers to the most advanced high-performance models at any given time, with OpenAI and Anthropic among the representative companies covered.
The bill imposes three core obligations on covered companies.
They must publicly disclose their safety management systems on their websites, detailing how they identify and manage AI risks, and must issue model transparency reports.
They must also notify authorities within a set deadline when major safety incidents occur.
The incident reporting deadline is 72 hours.
Enforcement falls to the newly established Division of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust (DIGIT).
The agency oversees large AI research labs and checks whether companies comply with statutory safety obligations.
Companies in violation can face penalties of up to $1 million (~1.3 billion won) for a first violation and up to $3 million (~4 billion won) for subsequent violations.
State authorities said they can take enforcement action against unregistered companies as well, but did not disclose the specific method.
A foundation has also been established for external verification of the safety policies companies submit.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul on the same day launched the New York AI Responsibility and Research Center at Binghamton University (SUNY).
The center will independently assess whether advanced AI systems operate safely, examine security and operational methods, and review corporate safety policies together with DIGIT.
Governor Hochul first announced plans for the center in January, backed by $55 million (~73 billion won) in donations and capital.
Speaking at a briefing that day, Governor Hochul criticized technology companies for justifying harm in the name of the AI development race.
"The tech moguls tell us that the AI future they envision is inevitable," she said.

"They say that if you don't join in, you'll be left behind." She added, "We are building a sensible AI regulatory model that puts communities before corporations and people before powerful technology."
New York State's move dovetails with regulatory trends in other states.

California's SB 53, which took effect in January, requires frontier AI developers to establish and disclose safety policies and protect whistleblowers, and mandates reporting of major safety incidents within 15 days.

Illinois's SB 315 also takes effect early next year and, in addition to similar safety and transparency obligations, requires companies to undergo independent audits of their compliance with safety standards.
In effect, incident reporting deadlines and review procedures vary depending on the state in which a company operates.
Separately from its oversight of frontier model developers, New York State is also strengthening protections for AI chatbot users.

Since last year, it has enforced a law requiring operators of AI companion services to periodically inform users that their conversational partner is an AI rather than a human, and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal thoughts or signs of self-harm.
Last month, it also enacted a chatbot safety law for minors.

The law restricts interactions that impersonate humans, emotionally manipulative responses, unconditional agreement, and behavior that encourages suicide or eating disorder behaviors, and takes effect June 1 of next year.
The new regulations are expected to increase the cost burden and compliance-system-building burden on large AI developers.
Disclosing safety policies, issuing transparency reports, and establishing incident reporting systems all require standing operational staff and internal control systems.

In particular, with reporting deadlines diverging between 72 hours and 15 days depending on the state, companies operating in multiple states will likely need to design their response systems to meet the strictest standard.

On the other hand, if a structure takes hold in which regulators and independent research institutions jointly review corporate safety policies, demand for external verification of AI safety assessments is also expected to grow.
